# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by successive technological advances, from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. Despite the efficacy of contemporary DES, concerns persist regarding permanent metallic caging of the vessel, late stent thrombosis, neoatherosclerosis, and impaired vasomotion [2,3]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support during vessel healing followed by complete resorption, theoretically restoring normal vascular physiology [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, clinical evidence, complications, and future directions for BVS technology.

## Rationale and Device Design

The central premise of BVS is "leaving nothing behind" [5]. By degrading over time, these devices may permit restoration of vasomotion, late luminal enlargement, and future surgical or percutaneous revascularization options [6]. The most extensively studied device, the everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold (Abbott Vascular), was constructed from poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) with a poly-D,L-lactide coating eluting everolimus [7]. Degradation occurs through hydrolysis of ester bonds, with full resorption typically within 2–3 years [8]. Other platforms, including magnesium-based scaffolds (Magmaris) and various polymeric designs, have also been investigated [9].

## Early Clinical Evidence

The ABSORB cohort A and B studies provided the first-in-human data, demonstrating feasibility, late lumen gain, and return of vasomotor function [10,11]. Imaging substudies using optical coherence tomography and intravascular ultrasound showed favorable strut coverage and scaffold resorption over time [12]. These encouraging early results spurred larger randomized trials comparing BVS with metallic DES [13].

The pivotal ABSORB II, III, China, and Japan trials randomized patients to the Absorb scaffold or the cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting Xience stent [14,15]. ABSORB III, the largest trial, demonstrated non-inferiority for target lesion failure at one year [16]. However, longer-term follow-up revealed concerning signals, including higher rates of device thrombosis and target vessel myocardial infarction [17].

## Concerns and Adverse Outcomes

Meta-analyses pooling randomized data consistently identified an increased risk of scaffold thrombosis with BVS compared with metallic DES, particularly very late events occurring beyond one year [18,19]. The thicker struts (≈150 μm versus ≈80 μm for contemporary DES) were implicated in flow disturbance, delayed endothelialization, and incomplete strut apposition [20]. Mechanistic studies highlighted scaffold discontinuities and late strut malapposition as substrates for thrombotic events [21].

Procedural technique emerged as a critical determinant of outcomes. Inadequate lesion preparation, undersizing, and insufficient post-dilatation contributed to suboptimal results [22]. The "PSP" technique—appropriate **P**redilatation, **S**izing, and **P**ost-dilatation—was associated with improved outcomes in registry analyses [23]. Vessel sizing was particularly important, as implantation in small vessels increased adverse event rates [24].

## Withdrawal and Lessons Learned

Given the unfavorable long-term safety profile, Abbott Vascular withdrew the Absorb scaffold from the commercial market in 2017 [25]. The ABSORB IV trial, which incorporated improved implantation technique and excluded very small vessels, showed more comparable early outcomes, suggesting that technique mitigated but did not eliminate the safety gap [26]. Extended follow-up analyses confirmed that the excess thrombotic risk attenuated after complete resorption, though the early hazard remained clinically significant [27].

## Current Status and Future Directions

The BVS experience underscored the importance of strut thickness, polymer properties, and procedural optimization [28]. Newer-generation scaffolds aim to reduce strut thickness, accelerate resorption, and improve radial strength [29]. Magnesium-based and novel polymeric scaffolds with thinner struts are under active investigation, and refined patient selection—favoring larger, non-calcified vessels—may improve outcomes [30]. Bioresorbable technology remains conceptually attractive, particularly for younger patients and specific anatomical subsets, but robust long-term safety data are essential before widespread adoption.

## Conclusion

Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds represented an innovative attempt to overcome the limitations of permanent metallic implants. While early studies were promising, randomized trials and meta-analyses revealed an increased risk of scaffold thrombosis attributable to device design and implantation technique. The withdrawal of the first-generation Absorb scaffold provided valuable lessons that are guiding the development of next-generation devices. The future of BVS will depend on engineering improvements, optimized implantation protocols, and careful patient selection.
